endorsements.quote: (1) Prospective, multi-site external validation with demographically diverse samples, reported with calibration metrics and subgroup analyses, should be required before any AI diagnostic or predictive tool is presented as clinically ready.

(2) Adherence to established AI-specific reporting frameworks (TRIPOD+AI, CONSORT-AI, SPIRIT-AI, DECIDE-AI, FUTURE-AI, as appropriate to study design) should be required by journals and funding bodies.
(4) Subgroup bias audits, including at minimum analysis by age, sex, gender, race/ethnicity, and socioeconomic status, should be pre-registered and publicly reported.
(5) Continuing consent models should be adopted for any tool involving ongoing data collection, with provisions for withdrawal and data deletion.

Disclosure of AI involvement should be treated as a component of informed consent: patients have both a right and a clinical interest in knowing when AI-assisted transcription, algorithmic risk scoring, or passive monitoring is operative within their care ( Park, 2024 ).
Data must not travel beyond its stated purpose, tools must collect no more than their function requires, and consent must be treated as a continuing process.

(7) Post-deployment safety monitoring - including adverse event reporting and regular re-validation as patient populations and clinical contexts change - should be treated as a regulatory requirement.
(6) Human oversight requirements should be specified in regulation for high-risk clinical AI functions, with clear accountability when algorithmic recommendations contribute to patient harm.
In practice, AI is likely to function best as a support tool within clinical decision-making, rather than as a replacement for clinician judgment in psychiatry.

Monitoring for automation bias should be built into the routine quality review of AI-assisted clinical tools, including tracking of rates at which clinicians override algorithmic recommendations and the outcomes of those overrides.

unlisted_practices: Specify limits on fully autonomous patient-facing AI systems in high-risk clinical contexts (crisis triage, medication initiation, risk assessment) in institutional policy rather than leaving them to individual clinician discretion.
Require economic evaluations of AI to account for implementation costs, data governance infrastructure, and post-deployment monitoring, not only technical performance.
Establish independent oversight of commercial mental health data practices.
Restrict sharing of mental health AI data with third parties, including insurers and employers.
Prohibit secondary use of mental health data, including model retraining, without explicit continuing consent.
Publicly disclose data retention and deletion policies for mental health AI tools.
Do not deploy AI in ways that displace human clinical relationships or reduce staffing in mental health services.
Avoid designing conversational agents to appear human in ways that exploit patients' relational needs.

screen.reason: This is a perspective article discussing clinical applications, limitations, ethical challenges, and governance needs for AI in psychiatry.
